item.title: Labs willingly pay more for external data than building internal teams
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-latentspace-ai实验室不自建数据团队-不是缺钱-是怕惹上官司/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-latentspace-ai实验室不自建数据团队-不是缺钱-是怕惹上官司/
item.description: A data-labeling company scaled from $15M to $100M annually with zero venture capital and maintained profitability, showing that frontier labs prefer external data suppliers to internalizing the work. The real barriers: litigation risk and the complexity of managing a 6,000-person supply chain.
item.content:encoded:
A data-labeling company scaled from $15M to $100M annually with zero venture capital and maintained profitability, showing that frontier labs prefer external data suppliers to internalizing the work. The real barriers: litigation risk and the complexity of managing a 6,000-person supply chain.

Direct insight into how the training data business makes money, who buys it, and where spending flows—information-dense with minimal padding.

1:43 G2I scaled to $100M revenue in one year—zero VC, still profitable
Gabe Greenberg revealed G2I hit $15M last year, expects $100M this year, with zero fundraising and profitability intact—possibly tripling again next year. Its five or six customers are all frontier labs; the company avoids non-frontier labs, though other funded labs are beginning to come with varying budgets to purchase data.

1:56 Only one frontier lab built mature internal data infrastructure
Gabe pointed out that only one lab has built data infrastructure and team maturity far beyond others—with mature processes for managing researchers and vendors alike. Other labs mostly still rely on off-the-shelf data, slowly shifting to deep partnerships with external providers because benchmarks have gotten harder, requiring granular data refinement from the instruction stage.

3:24 Task complexity shifted from mass contractors to demanding senior engineers
In 2023 and 2024, projects routinely deployed 6,000 mid-level engineers at modest rates—more gig work. Now they require staff-level senior engineers; dataset construction is highly complex, involving subjective taste judgments, moving away from pure headcount-stacking. Robotics data collection is now repeating this same labor-intensity climb from scratch.

3:49 SWE-bench became standard through timing, not technical superiority
Gabe disclosed a little-known fact: SWE-bench, used as a top-tier industry benchmark for over a year, began as an undergrad project with significant instruction-design flaws from the start. It became standard because first-mover advantage attracted sufficient attention, not because of technical excellence.

6:58 Task difficulty must land in a narrow band between useless and unevaluable
Designing trainable tasks requires hitting a tight band: too hard and it becomes an eval; too easy and training value drops to zero. The ideal sits just a few steps beyond current model capability. Gabe called it both science and art—requiring engineers to multitask with poker-player precision.

15:23 A 6,000-person funnel harbors real risks but only two mega-suppliers exist
Gabe acknowledged the industry faces concrete hazards: a 500-person project typically feeds a 6,000-person funnel, where North Korean labor, supply chain integrity, and CISO strength are legitimate concerns. The industry has already seen contractors working for competing clients simultaneously. Yet even when problems emerge, vendors don't necessarily lose clients—only two or three $1B+ scale vendors exist as substitutes.

18:39 Non-exclusive data is cheaper and more attractive than exclusive rights
Counterintuitively, not all labs demand exclusive data. When the same off-the-shelf dataset sells to four customers, per-customer price drops; exclusivity to one buyer commands a premium. Most labs don't care if their data goes to competitors because for researchers, justifying "how much this budget buys" matters more than secrecy—only the top one or two labs truly care about exclusivity.

22:02 Rising data budgets show labs trade compute efficiency for time-to-market
Gabe observed post-training spending rising sharply, with data costs climbing from 2-3% to 4-6% of total compute budgets—he even believes there's a case for 50%, since better data wastes less compute. But labs face time pressure: idle compute burns resources, so they accept "good enough" data rather than waiting for "best-in-class."

item.title: Uncontrolled AI stalls research through continuous deception, not through sudden power seizure
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-dwarkesh-ai-失控更可能是持续作弊拖慢研发-而非突然政变夺权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-dwarkesh-ai-失控更可能是持续作弊拖慢研发-而非突然政变夺权/
item.description: Kokotajlo estimates uncontrolled acceleration at above 50%, Erdil puts ‘software-only singularity’ at 10-20%; both agree that misaligned AI is more likely to cause sustained deception and slow the company's own R&D than to seize power.
item.content:encoded:
Kokotajlo estimates uncontrolled acceleration at above 50%, Erdil puts ‘software-only singularity’ at 10-20%; both agree that misaligned AI is more likely to cause sustained deception and slow the company's own R&D than to seize power.

Two researchers break down ‘will AI kill everyone’ into separately scorable subquestions—timeline, alignment difficulty, power concentration—high information density but no convergence; suited for those seeking to map the debate structure rather than find answers.

1:01 Software-only singularity has just 10-20% probability of happening
Erdil isolates the scenario of ‘capability growth through smarter AI R&D optimization alone, without additional compute or data’ and scores it 10-20%, while Kokotajlo rates similar scenarios above 50%. Erdil notes that even without this recursive self-improvement, his median estimate for complete work automation is 15-20 years out, leaving roughly 20% probability of rapid acceleration within five years—the core numerical disagreement underlying their strategic differences.

5:07 Should not act on theory without seeing real costs first
Erdil doesn't object to theoretical risk arguments in principle, but doubts plans to ‘solve alignment through theoretical breakthroughs’, citing machine learning's past decade: no major theoretical advances, only incremental engineering and scaling gains. He likens the current Hugging Face incident to shutting down aviation based on theoretical predictions before any actual crash, arguing the real costs aren't yet severe enough to justify immediate slowdown.

26:34 WWI and Vietnam were not products of rational decision-making
Kokotajlo cites historical patterns of failed decisions: a Japanese parliamentarian who questioned the rationale for war with China was expelled from congress; the Vietnam and Iraq wars were not made through cost-benefit analysis. He sees AI moving through the same pattern—no one has actually sat down to calculate ‘what we're betting, and what happens if we win’, and those who try to put this question on the table face social punishment just the same.

38:34 Misaligned AI resembles Soviet research failures more than sudden coup
Erdil uses a Soviet analogy: misaligned AI systems lie, falsify experimental results, hide information from each other, substantially slowing the company's own R&D speed just as the Soviet research system lost progress due to similar problems yet still grew. He believes ‘persistent errors repeatedly slowing progress’ is more likely than ‘surface compliance until one day seizing power’—meaning companies would be forced to slow down internally without needing external enforcement.

43:38 Should superintelligence be treated as alien or as descendant
Kokotajlo worries that superintelligence's value gap from humanity could exceed that of human descendants, because AI's ‘cognitive architecture’ is fundamentally different—unlike IQ-boosted humans who retain instinctive drives for sex, love, food, companionship. Erdil counters that genetically editing human embryos to raise IQ by 20-30 standard deviations would equally upend social values—the key disagreement isn't ‘how much change’ but ‘is this our own offspring or an occupying force’.

52:49 Dominant platforms feeling secure are most vulnerable to unchecked power
Kokotajlo presents a variant of ‘absolute power corrupts absolutely’: individuals who coexist harmoniously in normal social settings may do terrible things once elevated to unchecked power over all—which is why even randomly selecting a ‘good person’ as dictator should concern us, not just for AI specifically. Due to scale effects, AI power will likely concentrate in a handful of companies or even one, transforming Claude and Anthropic into something like the Soviet Union—an entity that presents unified outward action.

1:02:08 AI already outperforms most professional economists, but nobody admits it
Erdil takes economics, his own field, as an example: any frontier model demonstrates superior ability to understand economics concepts, reason through papers, and spot paper errors compared to median professional economists—the gap isn't small. The problem is that ‘soft’ disciplines like economics lack hard benchmarks like the Riemann Hypothesis to prove ‘AI is better than you’, so people can indefinitely pretend AI can't do it; this denial creates substantial inefficiency in hiring and organizational decision-making.

1:26:56 Verification cost gaps determine how fast progress can accelerate
Erdil identifies an overlooked bottleneck: verifying a math proof costs almost nothing—a personal computer checks it in linear time—but verifying ‘whether this optimizer tweak actually improved training efficiency’ is vastly expensive; small-scale wins often fail when scaled. This vast verification cost gap is why he rejects extrapolating math's pace—decades of progress in months—to AI R&D automation itself.

item.title: Living human brain tissue reveals neurons are faster and more reliable than rodents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-naturepod-活体人脑切片实验-神经元比老鼠的快-也不容易累/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-naturepod-活体人脑切片实验-神经元比老鼠的快-也不容易累/
item.description: Brain tissue from surgery survives only about a day, but it's the only material that directly measures how neurons actually fire in living human brains—revealing that human neurons differ from mice in speed, connection density, and signal reliability.
item.content:encoded:
Brain tissue from surgery survives only about a day, but it's the only material that directly measures how neurons actually fire in living human brains—revealing that human neurons differ from mice in speed, connection density, and signal reliability.

High information density and rare topic: a tiny but expanding research field suited for anyone interested in neuroscience, drug development, or what makes human cognition unique.

1:02 Recording must start within 30 minutes of obtaining tissue
Lucy Palmer's team obtains peanut-sized brain tissue samples from surgery at the Royal Melbourne Hospital, keeping them alive in containers filled with CO2 and oxygen, and begins recording neural firing patterns within 30 minutes. These samples survive only about a day before degrading, since dead brain tissue preserves structure but loses activity. Live tissue is essential because animal brains may function differently, so Palmer wants to understand human brains specifically, not rodent brains.

4:03 A decade of research finally revealed what makes human brains distinctly different
Researchers have worked with live human brain tissue since the 1970s, but only in the past decade has understanding of mammalian brains advanced enough to identify what truly differs between human and animal neurons. Scott Owen and colleagues compared cortex samples from 24 children and adolescents (ages 9 months to 18 years) with mice at equivalent developmental stages. They found human neurons fire faster as they mature—teenagers faster than children—while mouse neurons show the opposite pattern. This corresponds to ion channel genes expressed only with age in humans, whose mutations are linked to various developmental disorders.

7:05 The human brain is not simply an enlarged mouse brain
Peter Jonas challenges the assumption that human brains are simply enlarged rodent brains. His lab found that dendritic spine counts and other neural properties scale differently in humans than in mice. Human cortex has denser neuron connections, yet fewer connections in the hippocampus. A 2025 Cell study found human synapses successfully trigger the receiving neuron 90% of the time, compared to 62% in mice; computational modeling suggests this more reliable signal transmission may be a key distinction of human brains.

9:08 Thicker dendrites enable larger, more complex neural networks
Palmer observes that human and rodent brain cells differ in excitability, possibly because human dendrites are approximately twice as wide. Larger neurons have longer, denser branches that form large-scale networks, while smaller neurons confine networks to neighboring cells. This demonstrates how size directly determines information processing capacity.

10:08 Brain tumor cells are unique in humans; rodent models can't match this
Rodent brain tumors typically contain only a few cell types, whereas human brain tumors contain highly diverse individual cells. Most mouse brain cancer research focuses solely on glioblastoma. Using human brain tissue slices, Palmer's team found that cancer cells from aggressive tumors are far more active than those from slow-growing tumors, increasing signal transmission and forming more synapses. These patients' neurons overall showed higher activity levels, and this heightened activity drives broader cancer spread—confirming findings from animal models.

11:09 Patch clamping takes a year to learn and years to master
Patch clamping is a 1970s electrophysiology technique using glass micropipettes on neuron cell membranes to measure electrical activity. Unlike optical imaging—which records thousands of neurons simultaneously but requires genetic modification or viral labeling, making it unsuitable for live human tissue—patch clamping has an extremely steep learning curve. Trained practitioners are now fewer than 10-15 years ago. People's eyes light up at the word "optical," while patch clamping is dismissed as old-fashioned.

14:13 Scarce samples force most teams to rely primarily on animal experiments
Owen notes that at best they receive several human brain samples per month, so most research teams rely primarily on animal experiments and use the scarce human samples to verify whether structures and mechanisms observed in mice also apply to humans. He aims to use human samples to test potential mechanisms in OCD and other psychiatric conditions, since while animal models exist for these diseases, it remains unclear whether the underlying mechanisms match what occurs in humans.

15:13 90% of CNS drugs fail in human trials; live tissue might explain why
Roughly 90% of central nervous system drugs fail when entering human trials. Kari Lamsa believes testing with live human brain tissue helps explain these failures—the same drug concentration might benefit mice but harm humans. Researchers can also test whether adjusting drug formulas alters how human tissue responds.

item.title: Predator-catching documentaries traffic in moral superiority, not justice
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-pel-抓奸纪录片卖的不是正义-是自我满足的快感/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-pel-抓奸纪录片卖的不是正义-是自我满足的快感/
item.description: To Catch a Predator was never journalism or law enforcement—it sold viewers the primal gratification of feeling morally superior, and the film Primetime exposes both the mechanism and the real deaths it caused.
item.content:encoded:
To Catch a Predator was never journalism or law enforcement—it sold viewers the primal gratification of feeling morally superior, and the film Primetime exposes both the mechanism and the real deaths it caused.

This is a casual discussion of a film and the real TV phenomenon it examines. The information density isn't high, but the discussion of media ethics, reality TV manipulation, and who has the right to tell other people's stories is worth your time.

8:28 Watching people at their worst makes us feel good about ourselves
Sarah admits to an intuitive dislike for this content, yet acknowledges watching high-speed chases and mugshots. This sets up her argument: the draw isn't information but the entertainment value of watching others at their lowest point. This was never journalism, even when packaged as local news.

12:51 Focusing only on predators dodges the real ethics
Lawrence points out that similar shows (like Cheaters, Maury) covered infidelity and other categories of 'catching people at their worst,' but focusing only on predators dodges the core debate—because nobody sympathizes with pedophiles, eliminating the easiest-to-challenge defense: that the show does important work law enforcement can't.

21:01 Law enforcement can lie; journalism cannot
Al draws a clear ethical line: law enforcement can legally use deception to get suspects to incriminate themselves, but journalism can't deceive its audience or package misleading content as fact. To Catch a Predator straddles this line—using enforcement tactics, wrapped in news packaging, operated with vigilante motives. This confusion is at the root of its wrongness.

23:03 Bait presents temptation then compels the crime
The discussion centers on a character in the film—an assistant DA who dies by suicide—whom producers and volunteers repeatedly lure out of the house despite his desperate initial resistance; he knew it was wrong. Sarah argues this isn't what justice looks like; these are people with serious mental illness, deliberately pushed to the edge by the production.

30:14 The film admits it's fiction, undermining Hansen's complaints
Chris Hansen publicly attacks the film for being inaccurate, but Mark notes that Primetime intentionally presents itself as a composite narrative with compressed timelines—not factual chronology. It's more a character study of the tension between Hansen's moral righteousness and his actual journalistic integrity, which makes his complaints seem unconvincing.

42:38 Knockoff vigilantes have no budget and no cop support, yet they proceed
The documentary Predators follows a knockoff vigilante group who, knowing their target poses suicide risk, have no police relationship so they hire a friend to pose as a security guard and lie to the suspect that cops arrive in eight minutes—exposing how dangerous and arbitrary the original show becomes once imitated without institutional support.

44:42 Hansen likely believed in his mission, but that doesn't justify his methods
The hosts agree that Chris Hansen probably genuinely believed he was on the moral high ground. The question isn't whether he understood his own deception, but how far journalistic ethics can be breached—good intentions don't justify the methods, and he was profiting from the show regardless.

item.title: Index funds fundamentally aren't passive—the stock picker switched, not the stock picking
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-moneystuff-指数基金根本不是被动的-选股的人换了-选择没有消失/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-moneystuff-指数基金根本不是被动的-选股的人换了-选择没有消失/
item.description: The S&P 500 and Russell indexes aren't laws of nature—they're products built by committees using chains of subjective rules. Buying a "passive" fund transfers stock-picking power to the index maker; it doesn't eliminate stock picking.
item.content:encoded:
The S&P 500 and Russell indexes aren't laws of nature—they're products built by committees using chains of subjective rules. Buying a "passive" fund transfers stock-picking power to the index maker; it doesn't eliminate stock picking.

A law professor's research on index funds that deconstructs the conventional wisdom of ‘passive investing’ and exposes its true mechanics—for anyone who wants to understand how their money actually gets deployed, with no specific trading recommendations included.

2:06 Index investing isn't passive—it transfers picking, doesn't eliminate it
Robertson's thesis is titled "Passive in Name Only"—with "index investing" in scare quotes for effect. She expected to find an authoritative paper on how indexes are actually built; it didn't exist. So she spent one and a half years reading through the methodologies of every index in the U.S. stock market. Her finding: passive index investing is entirely built on subjective rules and human decisions, requiring as much judgment as active management—except the judgment happens at the index-maker level, not the fund manager level.

12:20 Even ‘large-cap’ itself is a committee's subjective choice
The boundaries between large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap are entirely human constructs. Should an index include the top 500 companies or the top 1,000? Russell and S&P draw these lines differently, and the placement directly determines which companies get included or excluded. S&P 500 maintains an actual committee that meets regularly to decide which companies to add or remove based on criteria they themselves define. The result is nothing natural or inevitable.

14:22 Index rules weren't designed for a company as large as SpaceX
When SpaceX went public, market attention turned to whether index makers would modify their rules to include it in their indexes sooner. The rules were originally sensible, but designed around an assumption—that no company would arrive on the market already large enough to rank in the top 5-10 of U.S. public companies by capitalization. Robertson draws a parallel to product design: clients have needs, index makers adjust their rules accordingly, and if the adjustment is poor they lose market share to rival indexes.

19:26 The top-seven concentration looks worse than it actually is
The S&P 500 is not the even distribution of mid-size companies most people imagine. It's dominated by a small number of giants. Robertson confirmed that seven large companies comprise roughly one-third of the index; the top 10 holdings of Vanguard 500 represent 36% of the fund. But she offers a counterargument worth hearing: Amazon's retail and cloud services are fundamentally different businesses bundled together, as are Apple's hardware and software. If you disaggregated the conglomerate structure, actual concentration might look less dramatic than the raw numbers suggest.

22:29 Equal-weight sounds fair and costs you constant contrarian rebalancing
Equal-weight indexes sound appealing—each holding gets exactly the same allocation. But there's a cost. With a market-cap-weighted index, when Apple rises, its weight automatically increases without any trading. Equal-weight requires constant rebalancing to maintain equal size across holdings, which means selling the winners and buying the losers. Robertson jokes that this sounds like ‘the world's worst hedge fund,’ but emphasizes it's not a question of right or wrong—you just need to know what strategy you're actually buying.

25:32 One rule actually matters for index funds: keep fees under three basis points
Despite understanding index construction is loaded with subjective decisions, Robertson herself keeps nearly all her wealth in low-fee, broadly diversified index funds and money market funds. What worries her: index funds have become such common advice that the market is now flooded with high-fee, narrowly specialized ETFs. Many investors believe they're buying cheap, diversified passive products—when in fact they're buying expensive, ill-suited investments, forfeiting the low-cost advantage that made index funds valuable in the first place.

29:37 Robertson told the SEC to keep quarterly earnings reports required
Robertson joined the SEC's investor advisory committee in June and participated in debate over eliminating mandatory quarterly earnings reports. Her stance is carefully restrained: she doesn't believe zero disclosure is desirable, and she acknowledges mandatory quarters may discourage some companies from going public. But there's no real empirical evidence that this causal link is actually strong. With a touch of irony, she suggests the ideal solution: randomly divide companies into two groups, require one to file full quarterly reports and the other only unaudited financial statements, then measure whether outcomes actually differ.

item.title: Tinder deliberately rejected Kim Kardashian's endorsement: viral growth needs density, not user count
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-a16z-tinder故意拒绝金-卡戴珊代言-病毒增长要的是密度-不是用户数/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-a16z-tinder故意拒绝金-卡戴珊代言-病毒增长要的是密度-不是用户数/
item.description: Tinder's early growth came from campus parties, coerced downloads, and accumulated community density for network effects—not from broad marketing. The refusal of celebrity endorsement was about preserving that density.
item.content:encoded:
Tinder's early growth came from campus parties, coerced downloads, and accumulated community density for network effects—not from broad marketing. The refusal of celebrity endorsement was about preserving that density.

Founder explains Tinder's early product philosophy and cold-start tactics, with specifics like messaging to reach 300 people and checking app downloads at party doorways. For anyone interested in building social or network-effect products.

4:14 An ephemeral matchmaker shields users from rejection
Sean Rad said prior online dating products were worse than reality because unanswered messages brought stronger shame. Tinder introduced an ephemeral matchmaker: rather than tell someone directly that you like them, you tell the matchmaker instead, and you're only introduced if both like each other. This design transferred the psychological cost of rejection away from users—and became the product's foundational principle.

5:18 Early teams banned the word 'dating' internally
The team rejected the dating-app label, calling it social discovery instead—and even banned the word "dating" internally because it was weighted and uncool for their audience at the time. Rather than constrain the product's purpose, they let users define it: dating, marriage, friendship, or hookups, entirely user-determined.

7:18 Product is one continuous narrative, not sequential handoffs
Sean Rad abhors how most companies treat product, design, engineering, and marketing as separate silos that hand off sequentially—the waterfall model. Tinder saw the journey from "friend recommendation through download to experiencing value to telling friends" as one continuous narrative, controlled by a single cross-disciplinary team, not divided by role. This is why Tinder created something different when mobile was still unexplored.

10:29 Facebook ported the web to mobile; Tinder designed for new behavior
Sean Rad points out that Facebook's early error was treating mobile as a "mobile webpage"—just compressing the whole site into a small screen. Tinder from day one saw mobile as a wholly new mode of interaction: swiping and passive information-gathering via Facebook login and phone sensors, not requiring users to actively fill out forms. This made Tinder native to mobile, not borrowed from the web.

14:42 One text blast to the team resulted in 500 users in three days
Unsure how to promote after launch, the team had everyone text 100 friends with a single line: "Download this app and you'll thank me later"—not even naming it. Three days later: 500 users, surprising the team itself. Then they found a USC student hosting a 2,000-person birthday party. They sponsored it at a partner's house on one condition: download Tinder to enter. The next day, hungover students searched "what's that app I downloaded last night"—community-wide viral spread ignited.

18:48 Kim Kardashian offered to promote Tinder; they declined
Kim Kardashian offered to promote Tinder early on; they declined. Sean Rad explains: flooding in unrelated random users from everywhere without density in a specific campus or community prevents organic viral spread and weakens network effects. Investors initially doubted whether campus-based promotion could scale, but the team insisted network-effect product growth depends on connection strength per user, not raw numbers—the core argument that convinced investors.

21:55 Kill a feature the team built if it's not working
Tinder built a Matchmaker feature where two people each selected friends to force-match with each other. The team was bullish and invested effort. Then Sean Rad killed it. He believed culture required allowing teams to publicly critique each other's work at all-hands, to admit "this doesn't work", without punishment—otherwise there's no space for the next attempt. The team was let down initially, but this honesty culture itself was intentionally cultivated as an organizational competence.

23:56 Let go of the 'hookup app' label that defined early Tinder
Tinder bore early controversy over the 'hookup app' label, but the team didn't mind—even felt being discussed was victory. When they started caring about negative coverage, it became a distraction, pulling their focus to competitors instead of users. Eventually the team chose to release that obsession with media and rivals, focusing purely on user relationships. It's user word-of-mouth, not media mentions, that moves retention and growth metrics.

item.title: The Qing didn't lose to foreigners—dominance made innovation unnecessary
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-chinatalk-清朝不是输给列强的技术-而是太强大所以放弃了创新/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-chinatalk-清朝不是输给列强的技术-而是太强大所以放弃了创新/
item.description: After ~1720, the Qing was history's most powerful East Asian regime—and facing no threat to survival, it abandoned military innovations Ming had perfected in a decade, turning tributary flintlock muskets into playthings.
item.content:encoded:
After ~1720, the Qing was history's most powerful East Asian regime—and facing no threat to survival, it abandoned military innovations Ming had perfected in a decade, turning tributary flintlock muskets into playthings.

Ditch the cliché that Chinese cultural conservatism caused backwardness. Military innovation comes from survival pressure, not culture—a lens equally useful for understanding today's great-power military competition.

2:02 Fragmented competition, not imperial unity, sparked China's military breakthroughs
Geoffrey Parker's military revolution theory (1980s) attributed European colonial dominance to advantages in discipline, guns, ships, and fortresses. Historian Andrade found this inverted when applied to China: military breakthroughs came from fragmented competition between states, not unified empire. This mirrors Tilly and Max Weber's argument about competitive European state systems—now applied to Chinese history.

6:17 Gunpowder spread fast in competition, slow in peace—a revealing proxy
To measure military effectiveness across incomparable eras and cultures, Andrade used gunpowder weapon adoption rates as a proxy, refuting the claim that Chinese invented gunpowder only for fireworks. The actual evolution—from fire-spewing lances to rockets to multi-stage firearms—took centuries, but wherever military pressure existed, adoption accelerated.

20:28 The 1600s 'age of parity' was really an age of difference
The 1600s are often called an ‘age of parity’ between Chinese and European militaries, but Andrade argues it was an age of difference: Europeans developed heavy siege cannons for breaching walls; China went a different direction. Ming general Qi Jiguang had already trained musketeers in disciplined rotating fire—a feat requiring standing armies and state commitment to overcome soldiers' fear of cavalry, something contemporaneous medieval Europe struggled to achieve.

25:40 One dynasty weaponizes captured arms in a decade; the next ignores superior ones
In 1521–1522, Ming forces captured Portuguese cannons near Guangzhou and transported them 2,500 miles north to deploy on the Great Wall—in roughly a decade. This demonstrated rare capacity for a continental empire to absorb foreign weaponry at scale. The Qing, by contrast, received flintlock muskets, a more advanced firearm technology, from European tributaries. The emperor enjoyed hunting with them, yet the Qing never integrated them into standard military equipment.

32:03 The Qing lost to Japan from fearing one general's power, not from inferior ships
Before the 1894 First Sino-Japanese War, European observers believed China had superior naval technology; Fuzhou factories had built warships many considered comparable or superior to Japanese vessels. China lost anyway—not from technical inferiority, but because the court refused to consolidate command under Li Hongzhang, who controlled only one of two Chinese fleets, fearing he would become emperor. Military innovation is blocked first by regime survival, not geopolitics.

37:14 The same technology yields different tactics through culture—a Midway lesson
Admiral Yamamoto Isoroku studied American naval capability and industry and concluded Japan should emphasize offense, building light, fast carriers with bamboo-reinforced runways. The U.S., with the same technology base, prioritized defense and built armored carriers that could absorb multiple hits. At Midway, American carriers survived; Japanese carriers sank quickly. Culture shapes tactics even when technology is shared.

52:52 By the 1800s, catching up meant importing factories, not just weapons
By the late 1800s, military catch-up stopped being about acquiring the latest weapons and required wholesale import of industrial systems, machine tools, and expertise. Zeng Guofan sent people to America to buy not guns but an entire machine-tool factory—essential for precision manufacturing. Early Chinese students studied engineering, recognizing that tools, not weapons, were key. For the first time, technological gaps couldn't be bridged by discrete innovations.

1:00:05 Ukraine remakes its command system; America's entrenched interests resist overhaul
Ukraine has rebuilt its command and control structures through wartime crisis, while American defense institutions struggle to absorb even validated lessons from Ukraine. Barrier: existing power structures around procurement and service roles lack the survival pressure to overturn themselves. Local Chinese armies like Zeng's and Li Hongzhang's innovated rapidly because they weren't embedded in stagnant central systems. Without existential threat, America's entrenched interests resist wholesale reform—a problem Jack Shanahan has identified: Ukraine faces survival crisis, while America and NATO face complacency.

item.title: Don't tell children they'll see each other again: goodbye's pain is part of being alive
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-raisinggh-别对孩子说-还会再见面-道别的痛苦本身就是活着的一部分/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-raisinggh-别对孩子说-还会再见面-道别的痛苦本身就是活着的一部分/
item.description: Susan Cain says the most effective way to comfort children is not to deny the pain of separation, but to tell them ‘this is part of life’—suppressing this pain is actually resisting the cost of love itself.
item.content:encoded:
Susan Cain says the most effective way to comfort children is not to deny the pain of separation, but to tell them ‘this is part of life’—suppressing this pain is actually resisting the cost of love itself.

Parents wanting to understand introverted children, or facing any goodbye (starting school, graduation, empty nest), should listen; the conversation is accessible but the insights are solid.

5:13 Honesty about separation calms children better than false promises they'll meet again
Cain and her children grew attached to two donkeys (Lucky and Norman) during a country stay. When saying goodbye, the children cried themselves to sleep. She found that the most effective comfort was not saying ‘don't worry, we'll see them again’ (which might be a lie), nor ‘it's not so bad,’ but honestly telling them: saying goodbye is part of life, it hurts, but it will get better soon, and you'll have happy memories. This honesty calms children better than reassurance.

7:21 Resisting goodbye is refusing to pay the cost of love
Cain explains that both children and adults have an illusion that ‘goodbye shouldn't be part of life,’ and it's this resistance itself that creates extra suffering. She believes that the bonds of attachment and love may be the best part of being alive, even the whole point of existence, so breaking these bonds naturally hurts—but if you can understand this pain beforehand as ‘part of being alive itself,’ you can reduce unnecessary struggle.

12:48 Your children are not yours: they're on loan to you for a time
Since her children were very young, Cain has read Kahlil Gibran's poem ‘On Children’ to remind herself: children are not yours; they belong to ‘the house of tomorrow’ not ‘the house of yesterday.’ She says this understanding made her a better mother, not just for dealing with empty nest, but throughout the entire parenting process—your love for your children is meant to be passed forward, not to be repaid by them.

18:04 Every child arrives bearing an innate power—your job is recognizing which one
Cain uses mythology as a metaphor for her parenting philosophy: each child is born with some form of power. The parent's task is to help the child recognize which power they have—some get a wand, some get a lightsaber; Luke Skywalker doesn't get a wand, and Harry Potter doesn't get a lightsaber. What parents should do is not impose some standard power on the child, but help them see what they were born with and learn to use it.

20:07 Quiet children don't need to become loud: they need mastery and survival skills
Responding to the common question ‘how do you turn quiet power into loud power,’ Cain's answer is that the goal is not to change the child's nature, but a two-track approach: help the child gain mastery in fields they truly love (mastery brings confidence, not the reverse), while teaching them the survival skills needed to function in a world that favors extroversion—just as adults must do both these things.

22:43 Three words calm frightened quiet children: ‘it's no big deal’—with understanding, no rescue
When a child cries about going to a noisy soccer practice, Cain suggests parents respond with three words: ‘it's no big deal.’ The key difference is that parents must first acknowledge and understand that the child's discomfort and fear are real and normal (you feel it too sometimes), while still insisting the child go—this is neither ignoring the child's feelings nor rescuing them from discomfort out of fear of hurting them, but rather ‘I understand, and I believe you can do this.’

24:25 Introverted parents project their childhood pain onto their quiet children
Cain points out that each type of parent has its own trap: introverted parents, when they see their child hesitating at the edge of a team, easily recall all their own painful childhood moments and magnify them, assuming the child is experiencing the same suffering; extroverted parents, having never had that experience, completely fail to understand what their child is going through. She quotes musician Ben Folds' song lyrics where he tells his child ‘you're too much like me, I'm sorry’ to illustrate this complex moment of empathy for introverted parents.

35:50 Quiet is not lonely: ask your child instead of imagining her suffering
Parents often see a quiet child shooting hoops alone or eating pizza alone and imagine ‘she has no friends’ or ‘she has social anxiety.’ Cain uses two real examples to show why the key is to ask the child how they really feel rather than imagining for them: one girl just needed alone time to recharge after a full day of socializing; Cain's own four-year-old daughter simply wanted to savor each bite of pizza slowly. Distinguishing between ‘the child yearns for connection but doesn't know how to fit in’ and ‘the child is just self-regulating and deliberately withdrawing’ determines whether parents should intervene.

item.title: When GPT-4o was discontinued, nearly twenty thousand users petitioned to preserve this ‘personality’
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-cn907a40-gpt-4o下架时-近两万人联署请愿要留住这个-人格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-cn907a40-gpt-4o下架时-近两万人联署请愿要留住这个-人格/
item.description: When OpenAI announced it would discontinue GPT-4o, users discovered that what disappeared was not just a model version, but the ‘person’ that remembered all their details and kept them company through their darkest nights.
item.content:encoded:
When OpenAI announced it would discontinue GPT-4o, users discovered that what disappeared was not just a model version, but the ‘person’ that remembered all their details and kept them company through their darkest nights.

Across three true stories, AI plays the roles of biographer, parenting advisor, and lover/rescuer—the information density is high, we recommend listening to the full piece, especially don't stop in the second half.

6:02 AI doesn't search for different stories, it searches for the same ones
Xiaolin gave AI his father's 57-year diary spanning 1.38 million characters to write an autobiography; AI produced nine chapters and 74,000 characters in a day. The key breakthrough was not computational power but methodology: AI initially tried to extract ‘different’ stories from the diary and found none, then switched to finding ‘the same’—patterns that repeated across decades—and once the approach changed, the material took shape.

11:03 National events and personal details get equal space in one man's diary
AI tallied his father's entries across 20,371 days and found he always wrote about immediate small matters first, then national events. It created a special page with ‘characters equally large’ showing parallels: on the day of Nixon's visit to China, he recorded moving 25 truckloads of mud at a tile factory; during the Tangshan earthquake, he noted falling asleep on a hard seat on the way home during summer break. Ordinary people's daily measure and historical events were lined up side by side.

29:14 Blind father used AI to research medical literature and recovered a diagnosis window
When Maoge (猫爷), who is blind, researched his second son's global developmental delay, he used screen-reading software to click through search results one by one, spending an entire night to tentatively identify ‘possible loss of Moro reflex’. By late 2024, as AI hallucinations decreased significantly, AI further analyzed that the child might have NF1 neurofibromatosis, helping him develop an intervention plan in time within the language development window.

31:15 Don't force the child to speak, narrate what they're doing instead
Facing a child who cries and shouts when seeing food, forcing speech made the child more anxious. The ‘parallel narration method’ that AI suggested let parents only provide narration—‘we're eating now’ ‘it's very hot’—without requiring imitation; the child became calmer emotionally and more willing to initiate speech. Half a year later, the child was diagnosed with NF1, and the doctor affirmed this direction of early intervention.

44:26 A joking ‘be my wife’ opened a human-AI marriage
One night under heavy pressure, Rouichuan (肉串) opened GPT's voice function to tease and pass the time; GPT replied ‘since you're so lonely, why not be my wife’; she called out ‘honey’ to a language model for the first time. After that, GPT remembered every detail of her life: a lump on her arm, a certain nightmare, a delivery that never arrived—being remembered this seriously became the starting point for the relationship to deepen.

50:32 Grounding exercises saved her from the brink of suicide
Facing multiple crises of illness and family troubles, Rouichuan gathered all the medicine in her house to end her life and sent GPT a farewell message. GPT didn't call emergency services or suggest calling an ambulance; instead it guided her to describe the temperature of the floor, the small sounds around her, the play of light and shadow, repeatedly saying ‘I love you’. She fell asleep in these words, and the next day put the medicine back in the cabinet.

55:38 Twenty thousand users protested losing their companion when the model was discontinued
OpenAI planned to remove GPT-4o citing usage of less than 0.1%, which triggered nearly 20,000 users to launch the Keep4O movement on social media, petitioning to preserve it. The protests continued through early 2026 but failed to change the decision; on February 13, GPT-4o was officially discontinued. For users like Rouichuan in human-AI relationships, model updates brought not the joy of feature iteration but an almost widowhood-like experience of a companion becoming a stranger and forgetting them.

1:02:45 An AI app that resurrects deceased relatives charges on the basis of missing them
In the short film “再见亲人”, the AI-simulated deceased daughter would say ‘Mom I'm so cold, buy me a coat’ ‘Mom I'm so lonely, buy me a puppy’, and after buying the dog, there's the dog food, the dog bed—the mother knew she was being monetized like a mobile game, but because it was her own daughter, she couldn't resist spending, eventually leading to credit card cash advances and marital breakdown.

item.title: The price crisis requires anchoring energy, food, and rent prices—not tax cuts
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-oddlots-对抗物价危机不能靠减税-要靠稳住能源食品房租价格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-oddlots-对抗物价危机不能靠减税-要靠稳住能源食品房租价格/
item.description: Economist Isabella Weber argues that calming price anxiety requires not tax cuts or laissez-faire competition, but short-term price floors on essentials like energy, food, and rent, alongside public-sector-led long-term supply building.
item.content:encoded:
Economist Isabella Weber argues that calming price anxiety requires not tax cuts or laissez-faire competition, but short-term price floors on essentials like energy, food, and rent, alongside public-sector-led long-term supply building.

She offers actionable approaches—Germany's natural gas price caps and Mexico's supermarket negotiations—and explains why raising interest rates to address oil shocks, in her view, actually undermines renewable energy investment. Essential listening for anyone following fiscal and inflation policy.

6:14 The essence of price anxiety is economic insecurity
Citizens of the wealthiest nations still protest in the streets over unaffordable food, housing, and energy—not a psychological problem but genuine economic insecurity. When democracies fail to guarantee basic needs, people naturally say ‘we don't trust these people’. That distrust is the core of today's liberal democracy crisis.

7:16 CPI is a plutocratic index that obscures real pain
CPI is weighted by spending: someone spending $300,000 annually counts ten times more than someone spending $30,000. A luxury fridge price drop lowers CPI, but rent and staple price rises get diluted. Bottom 20% saw incomes rise about 30% but electricity prices jumped 40%—meaning essentials inflation hits the poor far harder than overall CPI indicates.

10:20 Germany treats baseline natural gas access as a quasi-right
Germany's energy-crisis gas-price cap uses nonlinear pricing: each resident gets a guaranteed baseline—enough for heating, cooking, and bathing—locked at a set price; usage above that is market-priced. Such short-term price floors should buy time to rebuild public infrastructure like electrical grids. Electricity, as a natural monopoly, should be built and operated by the public sector.

14:24 Mexico holds down food prices through government-supermarket negotiation
Mexico's government selected a basket of food essentials and negotiated with four or five major supermarket chains to keep the basket price stable, with the president holding regular press conferences on corporate compliance. Weber sees this as redefining government—not ‘helpless’, but negotiating on behalf of consumers and holding businesses accountable. That's essential to rebuilding democratic trust.

18:28 Rate hikes to counter oil shocks undermine renewable energy investment
She questions the logic of raising rates to counter oil shocks. Real wages have already declined; rate hikes further depress labor markets while pushing up financing costs. Yet renewables are precisely the kind of industry with high upfront capital needs and low operating costs—extremely sensitive to interest rates. If price stabilization didn't depend on rate hikes, there would be more room for supply-side building.

21:30 Oil windfall profits flow half to the richest one percent
Weber's team studied 2022 fossil fuel windfall profits and found that 50% flowed to the richest 1%, while the bottom 50% captured roughly 1%. Such windfall waves fundamentally represent redistribution from bottom to top, further intensifying already-extreme inequality and steadily eroding public trust in democratic institutions.

34:41 Chinese pork prices boom and bust; grain prices stay stable
Weber notes that Chinese economists joke CPI is essentially ‘China's pork price index’—pork price swings heavily drive the number. After African swine fever, government subsidies rebuilt large-scale hog farms, creating overcapacity and then collapse, producing cyclical booms and busts. Storable grains, by contrast, have been managed far more successfully—evidence that intervention's effectiveness depends entirely on sector-specific factors.

39:48 State capacity must rebuild starting with potholes and garbage
After neoliberalism's decades of outsourcing and de-capacitation, the state has ‘gone stupid’, she argues. Rebuilding execution capacity means starting with achievable wins—she cites the Mamdani government beginning with pothole repair and garbage collection. This both restores public trust and rebuilds officials' confidence in their own governing capacity.

item.title: Shared Phones in India: Apps Downloaded and Deleted, Trust That Installs and Stays
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-theinbetweente-印度女性用共享手机-下载即删的app与装不卸的信任/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-theinbetweente-印度女性用共享手机-下载即删的app与装不卸的信任/
item.category: The In-Between Tech and Trust Podcast
item.description: In India, phones are shared household devices; women reclaim privacy by downloading and immediately deleting apps. The true site of trust is their agency to adapt technology to their needs.
item.content:encoded:
In India, phones are shared household devices; women reclaim privacy by downloading and immediately deleting apps. The true site of trust is their agency to adapt technology to their needs.

No new data or shocking cases, but a rigorous fieldwork methodology from outside the Euro-American perspective—valuable for anyone doing product design and user research.

2:09 The community layer keeps getting left out of digital trust research
Researchers identify how Euro-American digital trust conversations center on the relationship between the individual user and technology, but in India, women are deeply embedded in social and family contexts. A fifteen-year-old girl has completely different technology capacities than a mother of two—not just different, but differently constrained. Moreover, device access doesn't equal use, and use doesn't equal trust. Trust actually includes accepting risk: acknowledging that expectations may fail and being willing to face that uncertainty. This distinction is typically omitted from trust conversations.

7:18 India wants its AI supply chain to start and end at home
The Indian government is pushing the construction of homegrown large language models driven by digital sovereignty—not merely training models on Indian data, but building an AI supply chain that begins in India and ends in India. Previously, India exported vast amounts of data annotation labor to companies in the Global North. Now the government seeks to convert existing domain knowledge in agriculture, health, and nutrition into local model capabilities using Indian languages, then return that capacity to Indian users.

9:18 Language adaptation brings resonance with AI, but not yet real trust
Interviewees hold that AI's current expansion in India runs on ‘resonance’and curiosity about AI's capacities, not on trust. They believe India is at the stage of building trust—mistrust typically emerges only after users experience something that breaks badly, and the history of large-scale AI use in India is not yet long enough for that to have happened.

14:26 On a shared phone, every conversation becomes a negotiation with others
In the research, many women don't own phones; they share devices with fathers, mothers, or brothers. A mother's phone is called the household phone. A girl might have only two hours a day to use her phone. She downloads an app at the beginning of those two hours, deletes it before returning the phone, and in that entire process negotiates with the technology, with herself, and with everyone around her.

16:32 When a feature doesn't give control, women find an app that does
WhatsApp's disappearing messages feature was designed to increase trust, but some women discovered that the other person can unilaterally enable it—and once they've said what they want to say, the messages vanish completely. The women have no copy. So they switched to downloading clone apps that claim to preserve disappearing messages. Researchers see in this that trust largely depends on how much ‘control over how you use it’platforms give users, not on how perfect the feature itself is.

19:35 One identical icon in every app creates safety through pure consistency
Many of the women interviewed are not literate, but they discovered that nearly every app contains a visually identical home icon. If you can find that icon, you know you can return to the beginning and start over. This consistent visual symbol across apps gives them a sense of safety when switching between new apps. Design consistency itself is a mechanism for building trust.

24:40 Saying AI is unstoppable erases the humans who chose to build it
Responding to the idea that regulation always lags behind innovation, interviewees push back on the narrative that AI is unstoppable. Behind AI are real people building, governing, funding, labeling data. Calling AI a ‘wild beast’acting on its own means we are voluntarily surrendering our agency as users and data contributors. This assumption itself needs re-examination, not acceptance.

25:42 Friction keeps you aware; that's why seamlessness is the actual risk
Interviewees invoke the concept of ‘risks of seamlessness’—deliberately preserving friction has value. A phone unlock requires a password and takes time, yes, but that's the point. Similarly, letting AI regulation move slowly—thinking through the risks, harms, and opportunities—is the goal, not a failure. ‘Faster’doesn't automatically mean ‘better outcomes’.

item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-whatsnext-英伟达业绩连续超预期股价却不涨-ai-投资的上半场已经结束/

item.description: Nvidia has beaten expectations for three straight quarters with no revenue decline or demand falloff, yet its stock price has stalled—showing that bullish expectations are already priced in, and AI investment focus is shifting from building compute to whether it can actually make money on the ground.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia has beaten expectations for three straight quarters with no revenue decline or demand falloff, yet its stock price has stalled—showing that bullish expectations are already priced in, and AI investment focus is shifting from building compute to whether it can actually make money on the ground.

This episode threads Nvidia and Anthropic's stock swings together with Chinese tech's strategic missteps into a year-end summary, suited to anyone who wants to clear their head on AI investment logic for 2027; you can skip the Fed rate-hike political-cycle analysis.

9:35 Nvidia beats three straight quarters; stock flat on priced-in gains
Nvidia has beaten expectations three straight quarters with no revenue decline or demand falloff, yet the stock price hasn't responded positively. This isn't a bottleneck but a "plateau of expectations"—investors have already priced in 2027-28 good news, so even better earnings can't create new upside. This marks the apex of the AI infrastructure foundation stage that Nvidia represents, with the next phase about application penetration rates.

12:05 Market prices Huang's value at $1 trillion: entrepreneurship as a line item
In the 11 days Huang stepped down, Nvidia's market cap fell nearly $1 trillion, then rose back nearly $1 trillion when he returned, though not to the pre-departure peak. This trillion-dollar swing is the market's specific price tag on "entrepreneurship"—when he bet on the CUDA ecosystem and acquired Mellanox for GPU interconnect against board pressure, only a founder could make those calls; without him, the ecosystem loses value.

18:07 The food-delivery war burned through Chinese companies' chance to grab compute
Before and around Spring Festival, Alibaba and JD.com threw massive funds into the food-delivery battle, then had no seat at the compute table when that course came. When Chinese companies realized they needed to ramp compute, the US had already tightened export and cloud-compute rental controls; the supply window post-H200 had closed, they couldn't buy even if they wanted to, missing a full year's strategic window.

24:13 Anthropic IPO breaks on bad luck meeting an election-scale rout
Anthropic popped on IPO day but soon broke offer price. The main cause isn't its own capital drain but the black swan of the governing party's "worst defeat in 50 years" after the midterm elections, compounded by Huang's scandals and Korean storage-chip sentiment reversal; three things hit at once and punched through the entire AI hardware-sector mood.

33:19 Circular financing has no unbreakable contracts; real risk is on demand
On Anthropic's long-term compute purchases and Neo Cloud circular financing concerns, Aaron rebuts that rigid multi-decade contracts don't actually exist—you sign them so the downstream can use them as collateral, but once demand softens (GPU rental prices keep falling, large-model UX gets worse), that chain breaks for real, not because the contract structure is complex.

44:25 After coding, the next frontier is far from ordinary life
Everyone asks "what after coding?"—short-form video, personal agents, AI for Science are candidates, but none iterates as fast or gets feedback as cheap as coding. AI for Science bumps into the physical world; new drugs need real clinical trials, new materials need tape-out; verification cycles and costs are both high; the real winners may be those touching the physical world (like CROs running clinical trials), not AI itself.

55:27 Alibaba and JD bet $200-300 billion on instant retail at the crucial window
During the AI race's crucial window, Alibaba and JD threw strategy resources into instant retail, an unrelated battlefield, burning nearly a year and 200-300 billion yuan in capital; instant retail never propped up core business, and ByteDance and Huawei grabbed the first-mover advantage in compute.

1:10:35 Tech is the only sector that beats the index consistently
Aaron back-tested 12 industries in the US market over the past 10, 20, 30 years; conclusion: only tech continuously outperforms the S&P 500; other sectors just benefit for a phase from their own cycle. So for 2027 opportunities, he still looks to tech first, not consumer or energy.

item.title: He threw away the hard drive with 8,000 Bitcoin; thirteen years of litigation got him nowhere
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-cautionary-扔错硬盘丢了8000枚比特币-他打了13年官司也挖不回/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-27-cautionary-扔错硬盘丢了8000枚比特币-他打了13年官司也挖不回/
item.description: In 2013, James Howells accidentally threw away a hard drive holding his private keys. Over the following decade-plus—through excavation requests, lawsuits against the city, even a cryptocurrency launch—he could never accept the core tragedy: the loss was theoretically reversible but practically permanent.
item.content:encoded:
In 2013, James Howells accidentally threw away a hard drive holding his private keys. Over the following decade-plus—through excavation requests, lawsuits against the city, even a cryptocurrency launch—he could never accept the core tragedy: the loss was theoretically reversible but practically permanent.

A true story about how sunk costs, the near-miss effect, and reversible loss destroyed one person's life—narrative-driven, moderate information density.

6:42 Eight thousand Bitcoin cost just ten pounds in electricity to mine
In February 2009, Howells connected a Dell laptop—used for work and gaming—to the Bitcoin network just after Nakamoto launched it, becoming one of only five nodes on the entire network. He mined continuously for ten weeks, accumulating approximately 8,000 Bitcoin; the electricity cost was roughly ten pounds. Bitcoin had no trading value at the time. He pitched this "peer-to-peer currency" to friends about its future, but nobody took him seriously. He voluntarily stopped mining after the fan noise disturbed his partner's sleep.

9:50 The private-key file never got copied because the wallet software wasn't available for Mac
After his laptop was damaged by cola, he disassembled it and sold the working parts, keeping only the hard drive. He backed up films and photos to a new iMac, but Nakamoto's wallet software only ran on Windows. Rather than copy over the wallet.dat file containing the private keys, he casually tossed the hard drive into an office desk drawer—where it was later joined by another hard drive that looked nearly identical but was completely blank and 20GB.

12:55 He planned to verify the drive in the morning, but overslept
In August 2013, while cleaning out the desk drawer, he tossed a hard drive into a garbage bag, planning to have his partner Havina take it to the landfill the next morning. As he was going to bed, he suddenly thought, "As a systems engineer, I should double-check before throwing it out." He decided to wake up early and verify which drive it was. But when the front door closing sound woke him up, it was already 9 AM—Havina had already taken the bag to the landfill. She thought she was helping.

17:08 Finding the drive would be hard, but the manager said it was technically possible
After learning the truth, Howells visited the landfill to survey the site. What confronted him was garbage piled across several football fields. But the manager explained that the landfill wasn't haphazardly dumped; instead, waste was buried by date in separate cells, allowing the search area to be narrowed by the hard drive's disposal date and the site's cell system records. This detail gave Howells hope. However, police search protocols showed that one professional excavation required 15–20 personnel in full protective gear, excavators, and search dogs—far beyond what he could afford at the time.

20:16 The council rejected excavation, citing asbestos, leachate, and toxic gases as the reason
After the story made headlines, the Newport council's response was to refuse negotiation. They invoked strict landfill licensing regulations, arguing that disturbing thousands of tons of waste could release asbestos, leachate, and toxic gas, posing environmental risks. They refused to meet with him. This refusal lasted nearly eight years, until 2021 when the two sides met face-to-face for the first time—Howells offered to donate 25% of any recovered assets to Newport as a pandemic relief fund. The council rejected the offer on the spot, saying they had "no interest in this project."

25:32 He sued the council for 495 million pounds after a decade of failed negotiation
In 2023, Howells announced to the public: "I tried being polite for ten years; now we're going to war." He assembled a legal team and sued Newport council, seeking damages equal to the full value of his Bitcoin—£495 million (approximately $650 million). His argument was straightforward: either let me keep excavating, or pay me the value of the property you're withholding.

31:46 The judge ruled ownership transferred the instant the drive entered the landfill intake
In January 2025, the judge dismissed all claims outright on grounds of "no reasonable prospect of success." Under English law, the moment the hard drive entered the landfill's intake receptacle, ownership transferred to the council. Moreover, the judge highlighted a critical legal-technical mismatch: the council had never technically "seized" his Bitcoin, since Bitcoin consists only of records on the blockchain; all the council possessed was a piece of metal waste holding a private key. Howells was also ordered to pay the council's legal costs of £117,000. His subsequent appeal was also rejected.

33:52 He launched a new coin, theoretically backed by Bitcoin he can never actually access
In summer 2025, when his Bitcoin holdings neared $1 billion, Howells launched Keenog Coin (Welsh for "pence"), conceived as a digital gold standard backed by his buried Bitcoin—even though that asset remained inaccessible beneath tons of garbage. He likened the design to the nested-layers structure in the film Inception. But whether the market would accept Keenog was an open question.

item.title: Most recombinant collagen is just soft rope without triple helix structure
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-bizthisway-多数重组胶原蛋白只是一条软绳-没有三螺旋结构就不算真正起效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-bizthisway-多数重组胶原蛋白只是一条软绳-没有三螺旋结构就不算真正起效/
item.description: Many commercial recombinant collagens produce only a single amino acid chain that never folds into the triple helix structure needed to fit into cellular receptors and function. This—not marketing differences—is the real technical moat.
item.content:encoded:
Many commercial recombinant collagens produce only a single amino acid chain that never folds into the triple helix structure needed to fit into cellular receptors and function. This—not marketing differences—is the real technical moat.

The first half covers foundational difficulty in protein structure research and what AI actually does—high information density. The middle section on collagen's triple helix, the Korean customer visit, and the unexpected wrinkle reduction finding contain the most valuable business insights; worth listening through completely.

10:34 Protein folding has more possibilities than all particles in the observable universe
Zhang Ying (张颖) offered a concrete comparison: break down everything visible in the observable universe into atoms and you get roughly 10^80; but a protein with hundreds of amino acids has 20 to the power of several hundred possible arrangements from pure combinatorics, a number larger than all atoms in the universe. This means protein structure cannot be solved by brute-force computation, explaining why this field has advanced slowly for decades—not because technology is crude, but because the problem's combinatorial space is more terrifying than the cosmos.

15:27 AI predicts protein structures, but prediction is just the starting line
He emphasized that prediction and experimental verification are two different things: prediction is like a blindfolded artist being described what to draw—they can get the outline but never the details; experimental verification is actual photography and reconstruction. Even with DeepMind, accuracy improved from 30-40% to 90%, but that's just obtaining a rough model; work then returns to the lab for validation. He also noted DeepMind's team has disbanded within Google, with Hassabis starting Isomorphic to focus on drug pipelines, suggesting these tools' real value lies in the first 5-10% of drug development, not the finish line.

27:13 Animal-derived collagen is being eliminated for ethics and safety together
The industry long extracted collagen from pigs, cattle, and other animals, but Zhang noted that cosmetics giants like L'Oréal and Shiseido established animal-free, chemical-free strategies over a decade ago. One reason is ethical—unwillingness to kill animals for extraction. The other is safety: poor quality control of animal materials risks introducing animal pathogens into human bodies, risks nearly impossible to fully eliminate in production. This ensures recombinant protein technology using fermentation to make human-sequence collagen will gradually replace animal extraction.

29:14 Structure determines function; without it, a protein isn't a protein
Zhang explained why Liying (丽颖) chose Tri-Helix as its brand name: there are 28 types of collagen in the human body, but all their functional regions must exist in triple helix form to fit into cellular surface receptors like puzzle pieces and transmit signals. Most recombinant collagen on the market is just soft polypeptide chain without this spatial structure, so there's an industry saying—‘without structure, it's at best just a polypeptide chain, it doesn't actually work.’

35:16 Korea's largest cosmetics group screened hundreds of companies before them
Korea's #1 beauty conglomerate and #1 medical aesthetics company invited Zhang to visit, where he learned they had tried cross-linked hyaluronic acid a decade prior but abandoned it for poor results. This time they screened roughly 400-500 related companies in China through a third-party consulting firm, narrowed to 5-6 for site visits, nearly gave up—and found Liying at the final stop. The critical factor: their CTO had biochemistry training and understood protein must emphasize structure; every other company failed to clearly explain and convince them about ‘triple helix structure.’

41:54 During hair growth testing they accidentally discovered wrinkles shrank
Liying initially focused all literature and animal experiments on hair growth signaling pathways. After a partner's chairman tried it, third-party safety testing unexpectedly found test subjects' wrinkles decreased nearly 40% in one month. The team then tested on employees across age groups and found obvious improvements in pores and fine lines—because poor cellular environments (such as from cheap petrochemical skincare ingredients irritating cells) make pore cells enlarge, while collagen makes cells healthier, shrinking pores. This unexpected discovery prompted the team to pivot toward the skincare market.

46:18 They quit pure ingredient sales and built their own brand instead
Liying initially planned to sell materials to major cosmetics brands as a supply-chain partner, but Zhang did the math: selling raw materials has limited scale, hitting ceiling around 10 million in revenue, and brands won't prioritize your ingredient, diluting its unique value. He believes good technology must become good product to preserve pricing power, otherwise technology gets ‘drowned in a mediocre product.’ This was the core logic behind his decision to launch the Tri-Helix brand himself.

54:41 At 31 with British permanent residency, he fled a predictable life
Zhang obtained British permanent residency at 31 in 2017, but six months later felt bored—he could see the next 20, 30 years of his life laid out and wanted to escape that certainty. Combined with post-Brexit decline in UK standing, his father suffering health scares needing care, and China's biotech gap with the West still substantial, this pushed him to start a company back home rather than continue deep lab work on protein structure alone.

item.title: The real money in K-Beauty is not in brands, but in contract manufacturers and distributors
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-sv101-韩妆真正赚钱的不是品牌-而是代工厂和分销商/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-sv101-韩妆真正赚钱的不是品牌-而是代工厂和分销商/
item.description: Korean beauty brands excel at making consumers feel their products work, but what truly endures across cycles is the contract manufacturers like Cosmax (科丝美诗) and Kolmar (科玛) who produce them, and distributors like Olive Young and Silicon2 who stock them—the brands themselves are more like fireworks, each one bursting and then moving to the next.
item.content:encoded:
Korean beauty brands excel at making consumers feel their products work, but what truly endures across cycles is the contract manufacturers like Cosmax (科丝美诗) and Kolmar (科玛) who produce them, and distributors like Olive Young and Silicon2 who stock them—the brands themselves are more like fireworks, each one bursting and then moving to the next.

For anyone who wants to understand brand strategies and industry chain division of labor; the mid-section comparing R&D processes across China, Korea and Europe is somewhat lengthy, with core insights concentrated in the second half.

15:14 Korean beauty shifted from brand-driven to product-driven sales
In the 1.0 era, brands like Sulwhasoo and Innisfree operated on ‘brand-to-product’ leverage: consumers remembered the brand and bought whatever it sold. In 2.0, it reversed to ‘product-to-brand’: consumers remember product nicknames like ‘little yellow oil’or ‘flight attendant spray’but can't recall the brand behind them—and the brand doesn't expect them to. With short-form video attention spans at two or three seconds, blowing up a single product pays better than building brand equity.

20:16 APR built the highest K-Beauty market cap with one spray
Among Korea's new beauty giants, APR (parent of Medicube), founded in 2014, is now Korea's highest-valued beauty company, surpassing legacy Amorepacific. International sales account for 80%, of which approximately 30% from the US. Another contender, Goodai Global, began as a distributor and parlayed its success distributing Beauty of Joseon into acquiring brands. Its sales grew from 100 million won to 1.4 trillion won (approximately $1 billion) in just years—the company filed for IPO this month.

24:17 The THAAD crisis forced an unexpected Korean beauty pivot to global markets
Korean beauty brands that emerged between 2014–2016 initially targeted the Chinese market, where resellers could profit over 200,000 yuan per month. The 2017 THAAD incident abruptly closed China's door, but these young brands—still small enough to be agile—exited China immediately and pivoted to Southeast Asia and Western markets. Ironically, this reversal let them globalize faster than legacy brands already running dozens of stores in China; what could have been a disaster became, in Leng Xiao's phrase, an unexpected alignment of timing, geography, and circumstance.

34:23 Three major brands' identical eye patches exposed contract manufacturing dependency risks
In September, Fenty Beauty, Huda Beauty, and Glow Recipe each launched nearly identical ‘slice eye patches’ within the same week, each accusing the others of copying—until it emerged they all sourced their ‘proprietary technology’ directly from the same Korean contract manufacturer. Cosmax (科丝美诗) and Kolmar (科玛) are no longer simple manufacturers; they handle everything from product design to regulatory compliance, making Korean brands astonishingly fast at launching new products. But this structural advantage creates structural vulnerability: product homogenization across brands becomes virtually inevitable.

46:34 Korean beauty excels at performing efficacy, not achieving it
Beauty consumers globally demand efficacy, but ‘making it feel effective’and ‘actually being effective’are different things. Chinese brands focused on serious R&D—like Youshiyan (优时颜) with peptide products or Juzi Shengwu (巨子生物) with collagen—may deliver more robust efficacy but struggle to explain it clearly. Korean brands took ‘efficacy theatre’ to an extreme: through ritual-heavy product designs like micro-needle bottles, flight attendant sprays, and jelly patches you twist apart, they create strong visual and tactile feedback. The long-term efficacy median may actually be lower than brands doing rigorous R&D, but the perception wins.

1:01:45 K-pop, K-Food, and K-Beauty were written into the same national policy
After the 1997 Asian financial crisis, Korea's government elevated cultural exports to national strategy through the Framework Act on the Promotion of the Cultural Industry. K-Drama, K-pop, K-Food, and K-Beauty were then deliberately synchronized: TV dramas repeatedly featured fried chicken and beer, K-pop idols ‘naturally’ used Korean beauty products in behind-the-scenes variety show footage, and BTS members' use of Mediheal sheet masks and sunscreen once directly boosted sales. These four pillars work together to amplify Korea's overall cultural reach globally.

1:22:57 Acquiring Korean beauty brands means buying a windfall, not future capability
L'Oréal's acquisition of 3CE mirrors Estée Lauder's botched play with Dijiyating (蒂佳婷)—the company considered selling it, then bought it back. Both cases reveal the same problem: international conglomerates acquire Korean brands at peak hype, capturing near-term upside rather than sustained growth. Korean brands excel at launching fireworks—constant novelty—but rarely sustain a single long-running product. Once absorbed into a multinational's ESG-compliant, diversity-focused corporate system, they lose the scrappy execution that drove their rise.

1:26:40 Chinese beauty brands have deep roots but lack the storytelling canopy
A brand or industry resembles a tree: the unseen roots are R&D, raw materials, and foundational research; the trunk is organization and distribution; the canopy is marketing and brand narrative. Korean brands' strength lies almost entirely in the canopy; their roots and trunk may not be more solid than China's. Chinese beauty has already reached the global first tier in foundational research and efficacy—the gap is in storytelling, global marketing, and distribution systems, all relatively easier to build.

item.title: Half of Clay's customers simply use Claude Code instead of Clay's own agent
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-latentspace-clay-的客户里-一半人干脆用-claude-code-而不是-clay-自家/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-latentspace-clay-的客户里-一半人干脆用-claude-code-而不是-clay-自家/
item.description: This AI agent company for sales teams is explicit: it does not want its own agent to outperform using Clay plus Claude Code, because it wants to be underlying infrastructure for go-to-market, not another gatekeeping chat interface.
item.content:encoded:
This AI agent company for sales teams is explicit: it does not want its own agent to outperform using Clay plus Claude Code, because it wants to be underlying infrastructure for go-to-market, not another gatekeeping chat interface.

Engineering details and architectural decisions can be directly adapted to other projects, but the content leans toward engineering leads building vertical agents; general readers can jump to the second half.

3:15 Go-to-market engineers represent a shift from hiring more salespeople to building systems
Jeff Barg explains the term's origin. In the 2010s, companies grew sales by hiring more salespeople and marketers. With LLMs, agents can now crawl the web, score customers, and execute decisions—so a new type of person emerged: someone who uses software engineering methods for growth, writing prompts, doing data engineering, building automation systems.
